column1: 1:1|There was a man in the land of Uz named Job. He was a man of integrity, upright, fearing God and turning away from evil.|Retain the fourfold ethical description without claiming sinless perfection.
1:2|He had seven sons and three daughters.|Preserve the exact numbers and specified genders.

1:3|He owned seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred pairs of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys, with a very large household workforce. He was the greatest of all the people of the east.|Keep all livestock counts, paired oxen, female donkeys, and regional distinction.

1:4|His sons would take turns holding banquets in their homes, each on his own day. They would invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.|Leave each son’s day unspecified rather than asserting birthdays.

1:5|When a round of banquets was over, Job would send for them and consecrate them. He rose early in the morning and offered burnt offerings for each of them, thinking, “Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts.” Job did this regularly.|Preserve precautionary rather than proven guilt; render the blessing euphemism contextually.

1:6|One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and the accuser came among them.|Retain the divine-council designation and the accuser’s title rather than assuming a personal name.
1:7|The LORD asked the accuser, “Where have you come from?” The accuser answered, “From roaming the earth and walking about on it.”|Keep the repeated movement and direct exchange.

1:8|The LORD said to the accuser, “Have you considered my servant Job? There is no one like him on earth: a man of integrity, upright, fearing God and turning away from evil.”|Repeat the narrator’s fourfold description in the LORD’s appraisal.
1:9|The accuser answered the LORD, “Does Job fear God for nothing?|Preserve the question about disinterested reverence, echoed by without cause in 2:3.

1:10|Have you not put a hedge around him, his household, and everything he owns? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his livestock have spread across the land.|Keep the protective hedge and expanding livestock images.
1:11|But stretch out your hand and touch everything he has. He will surely curse you to your face!”|Retain the hand and face imagery and contextual curse euphemism.

1:12|The LORD said to the accuser, “Everything he has is in your hands. But do not lay a hand on the man himself.” Then the accuser left the LORD’s presence.|Preserve permission and its explicit bodily limit without softening agency.
1:13|One day Job’s sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house.|Keep both sons and daughters and the precise gathering place.
1:14|A messenger came to Job and said, “The oxen were plowing and the female donkeys were grazing nearby,|Begin the report before the calamity, preserving the ordinary work scene.
1:15|when the Sabeans attacked and carried them off. They killed the workers with the sword. I alone escaped to tell you.”|Keep human deaths and the survivor refrain alongside property loss.

1:16|While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, “Fire from God fell from heaven, burning up the sheep and the workers. I alone escaped to tell you.”|Preserve the messenger’s attribution of the fire, not a new narrator explanation.

1:17|While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, “The Chaldeans formed three raiding bands, swept down on the camels, and carried them off. They killed the workers with the sword. I alone escaped to tell you.”|Retain the three bands and repeated deaths and survivor formula.

1:18|While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, “Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house,|Repeat the opening domestic scene as the fourth report begins.

1:19|when a great wind came across the wilderness and struck the house’s four corners. It collapsed on the young people, and they died. I alone escaped to tell you.”|Render the collective youths to include the daughters and preserve all four corners.
1:20|Job rose, tore his robe, and shaved his head. Then he fell to the ground and worshiped.|Keep grief’s bodily acts alongside worship rather than treating them as opposites.

1:21|He said, “Naked I came from my mother’s womb,
and naked I will return there.
The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away.
Blessed be the name of the LORD.”|Preserve the puzzling return there and the familiar balanced blessing without forced novelty.
1:22|Through all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing.|Retain the narrator’s limited assessment of Job’s response.

2:1|Another day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD. The accuser also came among them to present himself before the LORD.|Repeat the council scene and the accuser’s explicitly stated presentation.
2:2|The LORD asked the accuser, “Where have you come from?” He answered, “From roaming the earth and walking about on it.”|Preserve the repeated exchange from the first scene.

2:3|The LORD said, “Have you considered my servant Job? There is no one like him on earth: a man of integrity, upright, fearing God and turning away from evil. He still holds firmly to his integrity, though you incited me against him to destroy him without cause.”|Keep the disturbing divine admission and without cause; do not explain it away.
2:4|The accuser answered the LORD, “Skin for skin! A man will give everything he has for his own life.|Retain the opaque proverb and its following explanation without inventing an origin.
2:5|But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and flesh. He will surely curse you to your face!”|Keep bodily specificity and the repeated challenge.
2:6|The LORD said to the accuser, “He is in your hands. Only spare his life.”|State the new permission and remaining limit plainly.

2:7|The accuser left the LORD’s presence and struck Job with terrible sores from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head.|Preserve the agent and whole-body extent without a speculative diagnosis.
2:8|Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself as he sat among the ashes.|Keep the concrete tool, bodily action, and setting.
2:9|His wife said to him, “Are you still holding firmly to your integrity? Curse God and die!”|Retain the wife’s direct challenge without adding a motive or caricature.

2:10|He answered, “You are speaking like one of the foolish women. Should we accept good from God and not accept adversity?” Through all this, Job did not sin with his lips.|Keep the rebuke as Job’s speech and the narrator’s explicit with-his-lips qualification.

2:11|Three of Job’s friends heard about all the adversity that had come upon him. Each set out from his own home: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They agreed to come together to mourn with him and comfort him.|Preserve all names and origins and the friends’ initial stated purpose.

2:12|When they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him. They wept aloud, tore their robes, and threw dust into the air over their heads.|Keep nonrecognition and the shared physical mourning.
2:13|They sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights. No one spoke a word to him, because they saw how great his pain was.|Preserve the full duration and silence’s stated reason.
3:1|After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth.|Distinguish cursing his day from the earlier challenge to curse God.
3:2|Job said:|Keep the speech introduction separate from the poem.
3:3|“Let the day I was born perish,\nand the night that said, ‘A boy is conceived!’|Preserve birth and conception and the personified night.
3:4|Let that day become darkness.\nLet God above take no notice of it;\nlet no light shine on it.|Retain the threefold undoing of the birth day.
3:5|Let darkness and deep shadow reclaim it.\nLet a cloud settle over it;\nlet the day’s blackness terrify it.|Keep darkness reclaiming the day and qualify the rare final term in a note.

3:6|Let thick darkness seize that night.\nLet it find no joy among the days of the year;\nlet it never enter the count of the months.|Follow the pointed rejoicing verb while noting the alternative joining sense.
3:7|Let that night be barren;\nlet no shout of joy enter it.|Preserve barrenness as the night’s wished-for condition.
3:8|Let those who curse days curse it,\nthose skilled at rousing Leviathan.|Keep the ancient chaos creature and curse imagery without rationalizing it.
3:9|Let its twilight stars go dark.\nLet it wait for light that never comes,\nand never see the eyelids of dawn,|Retain the striking dawn image and unfulfilled waiting.
3:10|because it did not shut the doors of the womb that bore me\nand hide trouble from my eyes.|Clarify the womb’s referent while preserving its doors.
3:11|Why did I not die at birth,\ncome out of the womb and breathe my last?|Retain the paired death questions as lament, not instruction.
3:12|Why were there knees to receive me,\nand breasts for me to nurse?|Keep the bodily images of welcome and nourishment.
3:13|Then I would be lying down in quiet.\nI would be asleep and at rest,|Preserve the imagined repose that answers the questions.
3:14|with kings and counselors of the earth\nwho built ruined places for themselves,|Keep the difficult ruin-building phrase without deciding it means tombs or restored cities.
3:15|or with princes who possessed gold\nand filled their houses with silver.|Retain the parallel wealth images beside death’s leveling.
3:16|Or I would be like a buried stillborn child,\nlike infants who never saw the light.|Preserve the grief-laden birth image without euphemizing it.
3:17|There the wicked stop their raging,\nand there the exhausted find rest.|Keep repeated there and the contrast between agitation and rest.
3:18|Prisoners are at ease together;\nthey no longer hear the taskmaster’s voice.|Preserve the social force of release from coercion.
3:19|Small and great are there alike,\nand the slave is free from his master.|Keep status differences and explicit slavery within the imagined equality.
3:20|Why is light given to those in misery,\nand life to those whose souls are bitter,|Retain the unanswered question and light/life parallel without adding a named subject.
3:21|who long for death that does not come\nand dig for it more eagerly than for buried treasure,|Keep the troubling search-for-death image in the speaker’s lament.
3:22|who rejoice with great joy\nand are glad when they find a grave?|Preserve the paradoxical joy and emphatic repetition.
3:23|Why is life given to a man whose way is hidden,\nwhom God has hedged in?|Repeat the opening question implicitly and retain the hedge’s changed meaning.
3:24|My sighing comes in place of bread,\nand my groans pour out like water.|Preserve the food and water images; note before my food as another reading.
3:25|What I dreaded has overtaken me;\nwhat I feared has come upon me.|Keep the doubled fear and arrival without specifying an earlier anxiety.
3:26|I have no ease, no quiet, no rest—\nonly turmoil comes.”|Preserve the three negations and final arrival of turmoil.
4:1|Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:|Identify the first friend’s speech and origin.
4:2|“If someone ventures a word with you, will you grow weary?\nYet who can hold back from speaking?|Keep the uneasy opening question and justification for breaking silence.
4:3|You have instructed many\nand strengthened feeble hands.|Preserve the prior help Eliphaz credits to Job.
4:4|Your words have raised up those who stumbled;\nyou have steadied buckling knees.|Keep the paired bodily images of support.
4:5|But now trouble comes to you, and you grow weary;\nit touches you, and you are dismayed.|Retain the accusation’s contrast with Job’s former help.
4:6|Is your reverence not your confidence,\nyour upright way of life your hope?|Keep reverence and integrity as the speaker’s proposed grounds of hope.
4:7|Think now: who ever perished while innocent?\nWhere were the upright destroyed?|Preserve the friend’s sweeping rhetorical claim as a question.
4:8|As I have seen, those who plow wrongdoing\nand sow trouble reap it.|Keep the agricultural sequence and appeal to observation.
4:9|At God’s breath they perish;\nat the blast of his anger they come to an end.|Retain breath and anger as parallel destructive images.
4:10|The lion’s roar and the fierce lion’s voice fall silent;\nthe young lions’ teeth are broken.|Supply fall silent to complete the compressed first line, retaining the teeth image.
4:11|The strong lion dies for lack of prey,\nand the lioness’s cubs are scattered.|Keep the distinct adult and cub outcomes.
4:12|A word came stealing to me;\nmy ear caught a whisper of it.|Preserve secret arrival and partial hearing.
4:13|Amid troubling thoughts from visions in the night,\nwhen deep sleep falls on people,|Keep the visionary setting without endorsing the vision’s authority.
4:14|fear and trembling came over me,\nshaking all my bones.|Retain the bodily intensity of the claimed experience.
4:15|A spirit passed before my face;\nthe hair on my body stood on end.|Preserve spirit or wind ambiguity in a note.
4:16|It stood still, but I could not make out its appearance.\nA shape was before my eyes.\nThere was silence, and then I heard a voice:|Keep the unrecognized form and silence preceding speech.
4:17|‘Can a mortal be righteous before God?\nCan a man be pure before his Maker?|Use before while noting the possible comparative more-than reading.
4:18|He does not trust even his servants;\nhe finds fault with his messengers.|Retain the heavenly servants and unspecified fault.

4:19|How much more those who live in houses of clay,\nwhose foundations are in dust,\nwho are crushed more easily than a moth!|Preserve the fragile dwelling image and qualify the moth comparison in a note.
4:20|Between morning and evening they are shattered;\nunnoticed, they perish forever.|Retain the brief span and absence of notice.
4:21|Is not their tent cord pulled up?\nThey die without wisdom.’|Keep the tent image and close the reported voice here.
5:1|Call out now! Is anyone answering you?\nTo which of the holy ones will you turn?|Preserve the challenge and heavenly holy ones.
5:2|Resentment kills the fool,\nand jealousy brings death to the simple.|Keep the paired passions and their claimed results.
5:3|I have seen a fool taking root,\nbut suddenly I cursed his dwelling.|Retain Eliphaz’s own cursing action rather than making it an impersonal event.
5:4|His children are far from safety;\nthey are crushed at the city gate, with no one to rescue them.|Keep the legal-social setting and vulnerable children.
5:5|The hungry eat his harvest,\ntaking it even from among thorns,\nand the thirsty pant after his wealth.|Render the difficult final term as thirsty with alternatives noted.
5:6|For wrongdoing does not sprout from the dust,\nnor does trouble grow from the ground.|Keep the two negated agricultural origins.
5:7|A human being is born to trouble\nas surely as sparks fly upward.|Use sparks for sons of flame with the ancient image explained briefly.
5:8|But I would seek God;\nI would lay my case before him.|Keep this advice in Eliphaz’s first-person hypothetical voice.
5:9|He does great things beyond searching out,\nwonders beyond counting.|Preserve the paired limits of human inquiry.
5:10|He gives rain to the earth\nand sends water over the fields.|Retain the concrete beneficent provision.
5:11|He lifts the lowly high\nand raises mourners to safety.|Keep both status and grief reversals.
5:12|He frustrates the schemes of the shrewd,\nso their hands achieve no success.|Preserve planning and failed execution.
5:13|He catches the wise in their own cunning,\nand the plans of the devious are swept away.|Retain the trap in one’s own cunning, not a condemnation of all wisdom.
5:14|They meet darkness in the daytime\nand grope at noon as though it were night.|Keep the paradoxical day and night imagery.
5:15|But he saves the poor from the sword of their mouths\nand from the hand of the strong.|Retain the compressed mouth-sword image and physical power.
5:16|So the poor have hope,\nand injustice shuts its mouth.|Keep personified injustice and the resulting hope.
5:17|Happy is the person God corrects!\nDo not reject the discipline of the Almighty.|Preserve Eliphaz’s interpretation of suffering as correction, not narrator endorsement.
5:18|For he wounds, but he binds up;\nhe strikes, but his hands heal.|Follow the plural hands reading and balanced actions.
5:19|He will rescue you from six troubles;\nin seven, harm will not touch you.|Retain the ascending numerical saying rather than literalizing a fixed quota.
5:20|In famine he will redeem you from death,\nand in war from the power of the sword.|Keep redemption and the two dangers.
5:21|You will be sheltered from the scourge of the tongue;\nyou will not fear destruction when it comes.|Retain speech as a lash and the promised protection.
5:22|You will laugh at destruction and famine;\nyou need not fear the earth’s wild animals.|Preserve the extravagant assurance in the friend’s voice.
5:23|For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field,\nand the wild animals will be at peace with you.|Keep the unusual nonhuman covenant partners.
5:24|You will know that your tent is secure;\nyou will inspect your dwelling and find nothing missing.|Render the final missing sense without importing a claim of sinlessness.
5:25|You will know that your descendants are many,\nyour offspring like the grass of the earth.|Keep the painful promise of children in its context after Job’s loss.
5:26|You will come to the grave in full vigor,\nlike a sheaf brought in at its proper season.|Retain the harvest-death comparison and uncertain vigor term.
5:27|We have examined this, and so it is.\nListen to it and know it for yourself.”|Keep the plural authority claim and direct closing exhortation.
6:1|Then Job answered:|Mark the return to Job’s own voice.
6:2|“If only my anguish could be weighed\nand all my calamity laid together on the scales!|Preserve the request to assess grief’s true weight.
6:3|It would outweigh the sand of the seas.\nThat is why my words have been rash.|Keep the overwhelming comparison and Job’s explanation of his speech.
6:4|The Almighty’s arrows are in me;\nmy spirit drinks their poison.\nGod’s terrors are arrayed against me.|Retain Job’s direct attribution and military bodily imagery.
6:5|Does a wild donkey bray when it has grass,\nor an ox low over its fodder?|Keep the animal questions implying a reason for complaint.
6:6|Can tasteless food be eaten without salt?\nIs there flavor in the white of an egg?|Use the traditional egg interpretation with the uncertain plant alternative noted.
6:7|I refuse to touch such things;\nthey are like sickening food to me.|Preserve disgust without assigning a specific referent to the food.
6:8|If only my request would be granted,\nif God would give me what I long for!|Keep the petition open until the next verse.
6:9|If only God would consent to crush me,\nrelease his hand and cut me off!|Preserve the wish for God to end his life without softening it.
6:10|Then I would still have this comfort,\nand exult in pain that does not relent:\nI have not denied the words of the Holy One.|Keep the difficult exultation and Job’s claim of fidelity.
6:11|What strength do I have to keep waiting?\nWhat future do I have to prolong my endurance?|Retain the two questions challenging prolonged hope.
6:12|Is my strength the strength of stones?\nIs my flesh bronze?|Keep the impossible bodily materials rather than paraphrasing invulnerability.
6:13|Have I not been left without help within me?\nHas every resource been driven from me?|Preserve the paired loss of capacity and aid.

6:14|A friend owes faithful love to one who is wasting away,\neven if he abandons reverence for the Almighty.|Choose the concessive reading while noting a possible accusation against the unkind friend.
6:15|My brothers have been treacherous like a streambed,\nlike channels whose waters pass away,|Retain brothers as Job’s relational appeal and begin the extended seasonal-water image.
6:16|dark with ice,\nwhere snow lies hidden.|Keep the winter abundance preceding disappointment.
6:17|When heat comes, they vanish;\nin the warmth they dry up where they stood.|Preserve the seasonal disappearance and emptied location.
6:18|Caravans turn aside from their routes;\nthey go up into the wasteland and perish.|Make caravans the travelers while noting the possible watercourse reading.
6:19|The caravans of Tema look for them;\nthe travelers of Sheba hope for them.|Keep both named trading groups and their expectation.
6:20|They are ashamed because they trusted;\nthey arrive there and are dismayed.|Preserve the betrayal of expectation without inventing rescue.
6:21|That is what you have become to me.\nYou see something dreadful and are afraid.|Use the contextual comparison amid the written/read difficulty, explained in a note.
6:22|Have I said, ‘Give me something,’\nor, ‘Pay a ransom for me from your wealth,’|Keep the denied requests in Job’s defense.
6:23|or, ‘Rescue me from an enemy’s hand;\nredeem me from the grip of ruthless men’?|Retain rescue and redemption as distinct parallel appeals.
6:24|Teach me, and I will be silent.\nShow me where I have gone wrong.|Keep willingness to hear evidence rather than conceding guilt.
6:25|How forceful honest words can be!\nBut what does your rebuke prove?|Preserve the contrast between honest speech and unsupported accusation.
6:26|Do you mean to correct mere words,\ntreating a desperate man’s speech as wind?|Keep the complaint that despair’s words are being treated as empty air.
6:27|You would even cast lots over an orphan\nand bargain away your friend.|Retain the severe social accusation and friend’s betrayal.
6:28|Now, please turn and look at me.\nWould I lie to your faces?|Keep the demand for personal attention and direct challenge.
6:29|Reconsider, please; let there be no injustice.\nReconsider—my righteousness is at stake.|Follow the repeated imperative and retain righteousness as the disputed issue.
6:30|Is there injustice on my tongue?\nCan my palate not discern calamity?|Preserve the mouth and taste images linking discernment to suffering.
7:1|Does not a mortal have hard service on earth,\nhis days like a hired worker’s?|Keep the assigned labor image rather than a generic statement that life is hard.
7:2|Like a slave longing for shade,\nlike a hired worker waiting for his wages,|Retain the distinction between enslaved and hired labor.
7:3|so I have been allotted months of emptiness,\nand nights of trouble have been assigned to me.|Keep the imposed allotment and differing units of time.
7:4|When I lie down, I ask, ‘When can I get up?’\nThe night drags on,\nand I am full of tossing until dawn.|Render the difficult night phrase as its experienced length.
7:5|My flesh is clothed with worms and crusts of dirt;\nmy skin closes up and breaks out again.|Preserve the graphic bodily affliction without diagnosis.
7:6|My days move faster than a weaver’s shuttle\nand end without hope.|Keep the weaving image and note hope/thread wordplay.
7:7|Remember that my life is a breath;\nmy eyes will never again see good.|Mark the turn to direct address without adding an absent divine name.
7:8|The eye that sees me will see me no more.\nYour eyes will look for me, but I will be gone.|Retain the shift from general sight to the addressee’s eyes.
7:9|As a cloud fades and vanishes,\nso one who goes down to Sheol does not come up.|Keep Job’s death claim within his speech and retain Sheol.
7:10|He will never return to his house;\nhis place will know him no more.|Preserve the personified place and permanent absence.
7:11|So I will not hold my tongue.\nI will speak from my spirit’s distress\nand complain from my soul’s bitterness.|Keep the deliberate refusal of silence and paired inner suffering.
7:12|Am I the Sea, or a sea monster,\nthat you set a guard over me?|Preserve ancient cosmic imagery and Job’s challenge to surveillance.
7:13|When I say, ‘My bed will comfort me;\nmy couch will ease my complaint,’|Keep the imagined refuge before its reversal.
7:14|you frighten me with dreams\nand terrify me with visions.|Retain direct accusation and the paired nocturnal terrors.
7:15|I would choose strangling,\ndeath rather than these bones of mine.|Preserve the specific distressing death image and literal bones, with the difficult comparison noted.
7:16|I despise my life; I will not live forever.\nLeave me alone, for my days are a breath.|Retain rejection, finite life, and the appeal for release.
7:17|What is a mortal, that you make so much of him,\nthat you set your heart on him,|Keep the question’s apparent dignity turned into distress by context.
7:18|inspect him every morning\nand test him every moment?|Preserve the relentless intervals of examination.
7:19|Will you never look away from me,\nor leave me long enough to swallow my spit?|Keep the bodily idiom for the briefest respite.

7:20|If I have sinned, what have I done to you, watcher of humanity?\nWhy have you made me your target,\nso that I have become a burden to myself?|Preserve the conditional challenge and pinned myself reading, with to-you alternative noted.

7:21|Why do you not pardon my rebellion
and take away my guilt?
Soon I will lie in the dust;
you will seek me, but I will be gone.”|Keep the request for pardon alongside imminent disappearance.
8:1|Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:|Identify the second friend before his rebuke.
8:2|“How long will you say these things?\nYour words are a mighty wind!|Retain the dismissal of Job’s words as wind.
8:3|Does God twist justice?\nDoes the Almighty twist what is right?|Keep the repeated verb and paired justice terms.
8:4|If your children sinned against him,\nhe handed them over to their rebellion.|Preserve Bildad’s harsh conditional explanation, not narrator endorsement.
8:5|But if you seek God earnestly\nand plead with the Almighty,|Keep the conditional appeal directed at Job.
8:6|if you are pure and upright,\nthen he will rouse himself for you\nand restore your rightful dwelling.|Retain the moral condition attached to promised restoration.
8:7|Your beginning will seem small;\nyour future will grow very great.|Keep the contrast in scale and time.
8:8|Ask the former generation,\nand attend to what their ancestors discovered.|Preserve the appeal to inherited inquiry.
8:9|We are only of yesterday and know nothing;\nour days on earth are a shadow.|Keep the humility claim and fleeting shadow image.
8:10|Will they not teach you and tell you,\nbring out words from their hearts?|Retain ancestral voices and inwardly held knowledge.
8:11|Can papyrus grow tall without a marsh?\nCan reeds flourish without water?|Keep the two water-dependent plants.
8:12|Still green and uncut,\nit withers before any other grass.|Preserve the sudden premature withering.
8:13|Such are the paths of all who forget God;\nthe hope of the godless will perish.|Keep Bildad’s explicit application of the plant image.
8:14|His confidence is fragile;\nwhat he trusts is a spider’s house.|Retain the unusual house image and uncertain fragility term.
8:15|He leans on his house, but it does not stand;\nhe clings to it, but it does not hold.|Keep the repeated failed support.
8:16|He is like a lush plant in the sunlight,\nits shoots spreading over the garden.|Make the resumed plant comparison intelligible without identifying its subject beyond he.
8:17|Its roots wind around a heap of stones;\nit searches out a home among the rocks.|Preserve roots and stone setting in the difficult second line.
8:18|If it is swallowed up from its place,\nthat place denies it: ‘I never saw you.’|Keep the personified place’s denial.
8:19|Such is the joy of its way,\nand others spring up from the dust.|Retain the apparently ironic joy and replacement plants.
8:20|God will not reject a person of integrity,\nnor take evildoers by the hand.|Keep the absolute assurance and supporting-hand image.
8:21|He will yet fill your mouth with laughter\nand your lips with shouts of joy.|Preserve the promised bodily expressions of restored joy.
8:22|Those who hate you will be clothed with shame,\nand the tent of the wicked will be gone.”|Retain clothing and vanished dwelling images.
9:1|Then Job answered:|Mark Job’s response to Bildad.
9:2|“Yes, I know that this is so.\nBut how can a mortal be in the right before God?|Keep the initial concession and judicial question together.
9:3|If someone wished to dispute with him,\nhe could not answer him once in a thousand times.|Preserve the overwhelming numerical imbalance and pronoun openness.
9:4|God is wise in heart and mighty in strength.\nWho has resisted him and come through unharmed?|Clarify the subject while retaining the challenge.
9:5|He moves mountains before they know it,\noverturning them in his anger.|Preserve mountains’ personification and divine anger.
9:6|He shakes the earth from its place,\nand its pillars tremble.|Keep the ancient cosmic structure as poetic imagery.
9:7|He commands the sun, and it does not rise;\nhe seals up the stars.|Retain both celestial restrictions.
9:8|He alone stretches out the heavens\nand treads on the heights of the sea.|Preserve the sea-heights image rather than importing a later narrative.
9:9|He made the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades,\nand the chambers of the south.|Use conventional constellation identifications with uncertainty noted.
9:10|He does great things beyond searching out,\nwonders beyond counting.|Repeat Eliphaz’s wording in 5:9 where Job takes it into his own argument.
9:11|He passes by me, but I do not see him;\nhe moves on, but I do not perceive him.|Keep the elusive movement and doubled nonperception.
9:12|If he snatches something away, who can stop him?\nWho can ask him, ‘What are you doing?’|Preserve power to seize and inability to challenge.
9:13|God does not turn back his anger;\neven Rahab’s helpers bow beneath him.|Retain the chaos figure’s name and subordinate helpers.
9:14|How much less could I answer him,\nchoosing my words to argue with him!|Keep the inference from cosmic power to Job’s legal helplessness.
9:15|Even if I were in the right, I could not answer;\nI could only plead with my judge.|Retain innocence’s inability to secure a hearing.
9:16|If I called and he answered,\nI would not believe he was listening to my voice.|Keep the disjunction between an answer and perceived attention.
9:17|He crushes me in a storm\nand multiplies my wounds without cause.|Preserve the source’s without-cause accusation, echoing the prologue.
9:18|He will not let me catch my breath;\nhe fills me with bitterness.|Keep breathlessness and enforced fullness.
9:19|If it is a matter of strength, he is mighty!\nIf it is a matter of justice, who can summon me?|Retain the difficult first-person summon me rather than silently changing it to him.
9:20|Even if I were in the right, my own mouth would condemn me;\neven if I had integrity, it would declare me crooked.|Keep the mouth’s self-defeating role; note the second line’s uncertain subject.
9:21|I have integrity! I no longer care for myself;\nI despise my life.|Preserve the bold integrity claim and rejection of life.
9:22|It is all the same. That is why I say,\n‘He destroys the person of integrity and the wicked alike.’|Keep the accusation fully in Job’s speech.

21:1|Then Job answered:|Mark Job’s rebuttal of brief wicked prosperity.
